differences.title: 1. MEMORY MODEL
differences.leftDesc: Rust enforces ownership, borrowing, and lifetimes at compile time, preventing use-after-free and data races. No tracing collector is required; deallocation follows deterministic drop semantics along control-flow.
differences.rightDesc: Go uses a tracing garbage collector over a managed heap. The runtime stops-the-world or uses concurrent phases to reclaim unreachable objects, trading predictable drop timing for reduced manual memory burden.

differences.title: 2. CONCURRENCY PRIMITIVES
differences.leftDesc: Rust expresses thread-safe sharing via Send/Sync trait bounds, so illegal cross-thread access fails to compile. Concurrency types like Mutex/RwLock carry explicit locking and borrow constraints in their APIs.
differences.rightDesc: Go provides lightweight goroutines multiplexed by the runtime scheduler onto OS threads. Channels plus select create structured communication, while the scheduler balances runnable goroutines to reduce blocking overhead.

differences.title: 3. DATA RACE DEFENSE
differences.leftDesc: The borrow checker prevents simultaneous mutable and immutable aliases within safe code, so data races are ruled out before running tests. Unsafe blocks can bypass rules, but are isolated and auditable.
differences.rightDesc: Go allows shared memory access without compile-time race guarantees. Instead, correctness relies on synchronization discipline and tooling like the race detector to catch unsafely concurrent access during execution.

differences.title: 4. LIFETIME & PERFORMANCE
differences.leftDesc: Rust’s lifetimes enable stack- or arena-like patterns without a tracing collector, producing stable latency and cache-friendly layouts. Drop runs deterministically, and monomorphization removes abstraction overhead.
differences.rightDesc: Go’s GC can introduce latency spikes, mitigated by concurrent marking and pacing. Escape analysis decides heap vs stack allocations, but object lifetime is ultimately governed by reachability rather than explicit drops.

differences.title: 5. BUILD ECOSYSTEM
differences.leftDesc: Cargo uses a lockfile plus semantic version resolution, and workspaces coordinate multi-crate builds. Features can enable conditional compilation, producing targeted binaries without runtime flags.
differences.rightDesc: Go modules use go.mod/go.sum to fetch versioned dependencies with minimal build metadata. The tooling emphasizes reproducibility via module sums, but feature selection is typically done through build tags.

differences.title: 6. CROSS-PLATFORM & LINKING
differences.leftDesc: Rust performs monomorphization for generics, generating concrete instantiations that may bloat code but improve runtime speed. Link-time optimization can further inline and remove dead paths.
differences.rightDesc: Go compiles to native code with a runtime-specific ABI and relatively predictable linking behavior. Escape analysis, inlining, and the linker’s dead-code elimination shape performance more than generic specialization.

differences.title: 7. ERGONOMICS & LEARNING CURVE
differences.leftDesc: Rust’s explicit ownership and borrow rules require upfront mental modeling, but the compiler feedback is precise. Refactoring often preserves correctness guarantees, reducing “works on my machine” concurrency bugs.
differences.rightDesc: Go’s syntax is intentionally minimal and the standard library is cohesive, making concurrency approachable quickly. The tradeoff is that some safety comes from conventions and testing rather than compile-time lifetime reasoning.
